{{Short description|1932 Australian nuisance wildlife management campaign}} {{pp-semi-indef}} {{Use dmy dates|date=February 2020}} {{Use Australian English|date=March 2018}} {{Infobox military operation | name = Emu War | image = Deceased emu during Emu War.jpg | image_size = 240px | caption = A man holding an emu killed by Australian soldiers | scope = | location = [[Campion, Western Australia|Campion district]], [[Western Australia]] | planned = | planned_by = Sir [[George Pearce]] | objective = Reduce the local [[emu]] population to reduce crop loss in [[Western Australia]] by the emus | executed = 2 November – 10 December 1932
({{Age in months, weeks and days|month1=11|day1=2|year1=1932|month2=12|day2=10|year2=1932}}) | executed_by = [[Australian Army]], led by Major Gwynydd Purves Wynne-Aubrey Meredith of the [[Royal Australian Artillery]] | outcome = Minimal impact on the overall emu population. | casualties = 986 emus confirmed killed. }} The '''Emu War''' (or '''Great Emu War'''){{Cite book |last=Shuttlesworth |first=Dorothy Edwards |url=https://archive.org/details/wildlifeofaustra00shut |title=The Wildlife of Australia and New Zealand |publisher=[[University of Michigan Press]] |year=1967 |page=69 |url-access=registration}} was a [[nuisance wildlife management]] [[military operation]] undertaken in [[Australia]] in late 1932 to address public concern over the number of [[emu]]s, large [[flightless bird]]s indigenous to Australia, said to have been destroying crops in the [[Campion, Western Australia|Campion]] district within the [[Wheatbelt (Western Australia)|Wheatbelt]] of [[Western Australia]]. The unsuccessful attempts to curb the emu population led to the deployment of [[Royal Australian Artillery]] soldiers armed with [[Lewis gun]]s—leading the media to adopt the name "Emu War" when referring to the incident. Although many birds were killed, the emu population persisted and continued to cause crop destruction. ==Background== {{further|Soldier settlement}} [[File:Fallow caused by emus.jpg|thumb|[[Fallow]] caused by emus]] Following [[World War I]], large numbers of [[Military discharge|discharged]] [[veteran]]s who served in the war were given land by the Australian government to take up farming within Western Australia, often in agriculturally marginal areas. With the onset of the [[Great Depression in Australia|Great Depression]] in 1929, these farmers were encouraged to increase their [[wheat]] crops, with the government promising—and failing to deliver—assistance in the form of [[subsidies]]. Because of the recommendations and the promised subsidies, wheat prices continued to fall, and by October 1932, the situation intensified, with the farmers preparing to harvest the season's crop while simultaneously threatening to refuse to deliver the wheat.{{Cite journal |last=Johnson |first=Murray |year=2006 |title='Feathered foes': soldier settlers and Western Australia's 'Emu War' of 1932 |journal=Journal of Australian Studies |volume=30 |issue=88 |pages=147–157 |doi=10.1080/14443050609388083 |s2cid=144598286 |issn=1444-3058}}{{Page number needed|date=August 2021}} The farmers' difficulties were worsened by the arrival of approximately 20,000 emus.{{Cite book |last=Gill |first=Frank B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zM0tG5ApO0UC&pg=PR26 |title=Ornithology |publisher=Macmillan |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-7167-4983-7 |edition=3rd |page=xxvi}} Emus regularly migrate after their breeding season, heading to the coast from the inland regions. With the cleared land and additional water supplies being made available for livestock by the Western Australian farmers, the emus found that the cultivated lands were good habitat, and they began to foray into farm territory—in particular the marginal farming land around [[Chandler, Western Australia|Chandler]] and [[Walgoolan, Western Australia|Walgoolan]]. The emus consumed and spoiled the crops and left large gaps in fences where rabbits could enter and cause further problems.{{Cite news |date=19 November 1932 |title='Emu War' defended |page=22 |work=[[The Argus (Melbourne)|The Argus]] |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article4509731 |location=Canberra}} Farmers relayed their concerns about the birds ravaging their crops, and a deputation of ex-soldiers were sent to meet with the [[Minister for Defence (Australia)|Minister of Defence]], Sir [[George Pearce]]. Having served in World War I, the soldier-settlers were well aware of the effectiveness of [[machine gun]]s, and they requested their deployment. The minister readily agreed, although with conditions attached: the guns were to be used by military personnel, troop transport was to be financed by the Western Australian government, and the farmers would provide food, accommodation, and payment for the ammunition.{{Cite news |date=18 October 1932 |title=Rain Scatters Emus |page=7 |work=The Argus |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article4504009 |location=Perth}} Pearce also supported the deployment on the grounds that the birds would make good target practice,{{Cite book |last1=Robin |first1=Libby |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W_9jMwwC4foC&pg=PT267 |title=Boom and Bust: Bird Stories For a Dry Country |last2=Joseph |first2=Leo |last3=Heinshohn |first3=Rob |publisher=CSIRO Publishing |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-643-09606-6 |page=256}} while it has also been argued that some in the government may have viewed the operation as a way of being seen to be helping the Western Australian farmers, as well as to stave off the nascent [[1933 Western Australian secession referendum|secession movement]]. Toward that end, a [[cinematographer]] from [[Movietone News|Fox Movietone]] was enlisted. == The "war" == [[File:Sir George Pearce.jpg|thumb|upright|Defence minister Sir [[George Pearce]] ordered the army to cull the emu population. He was later called the "Minister of the Emu War" in parliament by Senator [[James Dunn (Australian politician)|James Dunn]].{{Cite news |date=19 November 1932 |title=Over the Speakers Chair |work=[[The Canberra Times]] |location=Canberra |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article2318780 |access-date=10 January 2010}}]] Military involvement was due to begin in October 1932. The "war" was conducted under the command of Major Gwynydd Purves Wynne-Aubrey Meredith of the [[Royal Australian Artillery]]'s 7th Heavy Artillery, with Meredith commanding soldiers Sergeant S. McMurray and Gunner J. O'Halloran,{{Cite journal |last=Burton |first=Adrian |date=1 August 2013 |title=Tell me, mate, what were emus like? |journal=[[Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment]] |language=en |volume=11 |issue=6 |page=336 |doi=10.1890/1540-9295-11.6.336 |issn=1540-9309 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2013FrEE...11..336B }} armed with two [[Lewis gun]]s{{Cite book |last=Arthur |first=Jay Mary |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kr7ddMAUnqUC&pg=PA123 |title=The Default Country: A Lexical Cartography of Twentieth-century Australia |publisher=UNSW Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-86840-542-1 |pages=123–124}} and 10,000 rounds of ammunition. The operation was delayed by a period of rainfall that caused the [[Emu|emus]] to scatter over a wider area. The rain ceased by 2 November 1932, whereupon the troops were deployed with orders to assist the farmers and, according to a newspaper account, to collect 100 emu skins so that their feathers could be used to make hats for [[Australian Light Horse|light horsemen]].{{Cite news |date=3 November 1932 |title=Machine Guns Sent Against Emu Pests |page=2 |work=The Argus |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article2315329 |location=Perth}} ===First attempt=== On 2 November, the men travelled to [[Campion, Western Australia|Campion]], where some 50 emus were sighted. As the birds were out of range of the guns, the local settlers attempted to herd the emus into an [[ambush]], but the birds split into small groups and ran so that they were difficult to target. Nevertheless, while the first fusillade from the machine guns was ineffective due to the range, a second round of gunfire was able to kill "a number" of birds. Later the same day a small flock was encountered, and "perhaps a dozen" birds were killed. The next significant event was on 4 November. Meredith had established an ambush near a local [[dam]], and more than 1,000 emus were spotted heading towards their position. This time, the gunners waited until the birds were in close proximity before opening fire. The gun jammed after only 12 birds were killed, and the remainder scattered before any more could be shot. No more birds were sighted that day. In the days that followed, Meredith chose to move further south, where the birds were "reported to be fairly tame",''West Australian'', 4 March 1932, quoted in Johnson (2006), p. 152. but there was only limited success despite his efforts. By the fourth day of the campaign, army observers noted that "each pack seems to have its own leader now—a big black-plumed bird which stands fully {{convert|6|ft|spell=in|disp=sqbr}} high and keeps watch while his mates carry out their work of destruction and warns them of our approach".{{Cite news |date=5 July 1953 |title=New Strategy in a War on the Emu, by a Special Correspondent |page=13 |location=[[Sydney]], [[New South Wales]] |work=[[The Sun-Herald|Sunday Herald]] |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article18516559 |quote=[A] variety of methods to control the menace ... have met at best with mixed success, and even at times have resulted in such farcical and humiliating defeats that there are many officials and experts to-day in the State who cannot bear to be reminded of the outcome of some of their more ambitious efforts at emu destruction. Among the failures was a military expedition carried out by a Royal Australian Artillery detachment employing a range of military technique, including mobile warfare strategy and guerrilla tactics. This, the most ambitious project in the history of Western Australia's emu war, was the one which failed most miserably, and which brought for the bird its most complete victory; and the incongruity of the whole thing even had the effect, for once, of arousing public sympathy for the emu.}} At one stage, Meredith even went so far as to mount one of the guns on a truck, a move that proved to be ineffective, as the truck was unable to gain on the birds, and the ride was so rough that the gunner was unable to fire any shots. By 8 November, six days after the first engagement, 2,500 rounds of ammunition had been fired. The number of birds killed is uncertain: one account estimates that it was 50 birds, but other accounts range from 200 to 500, the latter figure being provided by the settlers. Meredith's official report noted that his men had suffered no casualties, except for their dignity. Summarising the culls, ornithologist [[Dominic Serventy]] commented: {{Blockquote | style=font-size:100% | The machine-gunners' dreams of point-blank fire into serried masses of Emus were soon dissipated. The Emu command had evidently ordered guerrilla tactics, and its unwieldy army soon split up into innumerable small units that made use of the military equipment uneconomic. A crestfallen field force therefore withdrew from the combat area after about a month.{{Cite web |editor1=John P. Rafferty |editor2=Richard Pallardy |year=2009 |title=casuariiform |url=https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/98874/casuariiform |access-date=16 August 2009 |publisher=Encyclopedia Britannica |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110205132607/https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/98874/casuariiform |archive-date=5 February 2011}}{{cite web | title=Pickering Brook Heritage Group- Heritage Sites | url=https://old.pickeringbrookheritagegroup.com.au/misc1.html#:~:text=As%20the%20naturalist%20Dominic%20Serventy,use%20of%20military%20equipment%20uneconomic. }}}} On 8 November, members in the [[House of Representatives (Australia)|Australian House of Representatives]] discussed the operation. Following the negative coverage of the events in the local media, which included claims that "only a few" emus had died, Pearce withdrew the military personnel and the guns on 8 November.{{Cite news |date=10 November 1932 |title=War on Emus |page=8 |work=The Argus |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/4507996}}{{Cite news |date=12 November 1932 |title=Emu War Again |page=1 |work=The Canberra Times |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/2317086 }} After the withdrawal, Major Meredith compared the emus to [[Zulu people|Zulus]] and commented on the striking manoeuvrability of the emus, even while badly wounded. {{Blockquote | style=font-size:100% | If we had a military division with the bullet-carrying capacity of these birds, it would face any army in the world ... They can face machine guns with the invulnerability of tanks. They are like Zulus whom even [[Expanding bullet|dum-dum bullets]] could not stop.}} === Second attempt === [[File:Joseph Lyons seated.jpg|thumb|upright|In November 1932, during parliamentary [[question time]], Prime Minister [[Joseph Lyons]] (pictured) was mockingly asked by [[Lang Labor]] MP [[Rowley James]] whether a medal would be struck for the soldiers.{{cite news|url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/32587930|title=Questions in Representatives|newspaper=The West Australian|date=9 November 1932}}]] After the withdrawal of the military, the emu attacks on crops continued. Farmers again asked for support, citing the hot weather and drought that brought emus invading farms in the thousands. [[James Mitchell (Australian politician)|James Mitchell]], the [[Premier of Western Australia]], lent his strong support for the renewal of military assistance. At the same time, a report from the Base Commander was issued that indicated 300 emus had been killed in the initial operation. Acting on the requests and the Base Commander's report, by 12 November the Minister of Defence approved a resumption of military efforts. He defended the decision in the [[Australian Senate|Senate]], explaining why the soldiers were necessary to combat the serious agricultural threat of the large emu population. Although the military had agreed to lend the guns to the Western Australian government on the expectation that they would provide the necessary people, Meredith was once again placed in the field due to an apparent lack of experienced machine gunners in the state. Taking to the field on 13 November 1932, the military found a degree of success over the first two days, with approximately 40 emus killed. The third day, 15 November, proved to be far less successful, but by 2 December, the soldiers were killing approximately 100 emus per week. Meredith was recalled on 10 December, and in his report, he claimed 986 confirmed kills with 9,860 rounds, at a rate of exactly 10 rounds per confirmed kill. In addition, Meredith claimed exactly 2,500 wounded birds had also died from their injuries. Historian Greg Beyer wrote, "This figure, however, is highly disputed and is likely to be very inflated."{{Cite web |last=Beyer |first=Greg |date=September 15, 2023 |title=The Great Emu War: When Australians Lost to Flightless Birds |url=https://www.thecollector.com/great-emu-war/ |publisher=The Collector |access-date=June 4, 2025}} In assessing the success of the cull, an article in the ''[[Coolgardie Miner]]'' on 23 August 1935 reported that although the use of machine guns had been "criticised in many quarters, the method proved effective and saved what remained of the wheat".{{Cite news |date=23 August 1935 |title=Another "Emu War"? |work=[[Coolgardie Miner]] |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/217998228?searchTerm=emu%20war%20effective&searchLimits= |access-date=9 December 2019 |via=[[Trove]]}} == Aftermath == Despite the problems encountered with the cull, the farmers of the region once again requested military assistance in 1934, 1943, and 1948, but were turned down by the government.{{Cite web |date=3 July 1943 |title=Request to Use Bombs to Kill Emus |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article55872191 |pages=12 |via=Trove |newspaper=The Mail |location=Perth}} Instead, the bounty system that had been instigated in 1923 was continued, and this proved to be effective: 57,034 bounties were claimed over a six-month period in 1934. By December 1932, word of the Emu War had spread, reaching the United Kingdom. Some conservationists there protested the cull as "extermination of the rare emu".{{Cite book |last=Jenkins |first=C.F.H. |title=The Wanderings of an Entomologist |publisher=[[Cornell University Press]] |year=1988 |isbn=978-0-7316-2888-9 |page=8}} [[Dominic Serventy]] and [[Hubert Whittell]], the eminent Australian ornithologists, described the "war" as "an attempt at the mass destruction of the birds".{{Cite book |last1=Serventy |first1=Dominic Louis |title=A Handbook of the Birds of Western Australia (with the exception of the Kimberley Division) |title-link=Birds of Western Australia (book) |last2=Hubert Massey Whittell |publisher=Patersons Press; Original: [[University of Wisconsin Press]] |year=1948 |page=63 |author-link=Dominic Serventy |author-link2=Hubert Massey Whittell}}{{Cite web |last=Gore |first=Jasper Garner |date=2 November 2016 |title=Looking Back: Australia's Emu Wars |url=https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/topics/wildlife/2016/10/on-this-day-the-emu-wars-begin/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180421023023/http://www.australiangeographic.com.au/blogs/on-this-day/2016/11/on-this-day-the-emu-wars-begin |archive-date=21 April 2018 |access-date=29 October 2017 |publisher=Australian Geographic}}{{Cite web |last=Crew |first=Bec |date=4 August 2014 |title=The Great Emu War: In which some large, flightless birds unwittingly foiled the Australian Army |url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/running-ponies/the-great-emu-war-in-which-some-large-flightless-birds-unwittingly-foiled-the-australian-army |access-date=2 November 2020 |publisher=Scientific American Blogs|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20230208193043/https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/running-ponies/the-great-emu-war-in-which-some-large-flightless-birds-unwittingly-foiled-the-australian-army/|archive-date=February 8, 2023}} Throughout 1930 and onward, [[Pest-exclusion fence|exclusion barrier fencing]] became a popular means of keeping emus out of agricultural areas (in addition to other [[vermin]], such as [[dingo]]es and [[rabbit]]s).{{Cite journal |last=McKnight |first=Tom |date=July 1969 |title=Barrier Fencing for Vermin Control in Australia |journal=Geographical Review |volume=59 |issue=3 |pages=330–347 |doi=10.2307/213480 |jstor=213480|bibcode=1969GeoRv..59..330M }} In November 1950, [[Hugh Leslie]] raised the issues of emus in federal parliament and urged Army Minister [[Josiah Francis]] to release a quantity of .303 ammunition from the army for the use of farmers. The minister approved the release of 500,000 rounds of ammunition.{{Cite news |date=30 November 1950 |title=Control of emus |work=[[Coolgardie Miner]] |url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/218049072|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20230404164606/https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/218049072|archive-date=April 4, 2023}} == Legacy == An action-comedy film, titled ''The Emu War'', premiered at [[Monster Fest]] on 22 October 2023.{{Cite news |last=Shepherd |first=Tory |date=2023-10-06 |title=Australia's emu war: John Cleese outrun in race to shoot movie of how flightless birds thwarted army's machine guns |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2023/oct/06/australias-emu-war-john-cleese-outrun-in-race-to-shoot-movie-of-how-flightless-birds-thwarted-armys-machine-guns |access-date=2023-10-09 |issn=0261-3077}}{{Cite web |date=2023-09-08 |title=Trailer Drops for Monster Fest 2023 Official Selection THE EMU WAR |url=https://www.monsterfest.com.au/umbrella-theemuwar-teaser/ |access-date=2023-10-09 |website=Monster Fest |language=en-US}} Another action-comedy movie retelling of the events called ''The Great Emu War'', written by [[John Cleese]], Monty Franklin, [[Rob Schneider]], Camilla Cleese, and [[Jim Jefferies]], was aiming to begin production in 2023 or 2024.{{Cite web |date=2021-03-08 |title=British and US comedy legends bring bizarre chapter of Australian history to big screen |url=https://7news.com.au/entertainment/john-cleese-rob-schneider-write-script-for-australian-emu-war-movie-c-2307774 |access-date=2021-06-16 |website=7NEWS.com.au |language=en|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220731140656/https://7news.com.au/entertainment/john-cleese-rob-schneider-write-script-for-australian-emu-war-movie-c-2307774|archive-date=July 31, 2022}}{{needs update |reason=Its 2024 now, and is it still going ahead after the Monster Fest? (I hope it does!) |date=January 2024}} == See also == * [[Brumby shooting]] * [[Dingo Fence]] * [[Eliminate Sparrows campaign]] * [[Rabbits in Australia]] == References == {{Reflist}} ==External links== * [https://web.archive.org/web/20070929092700/http://www.naturebase.net/pdf/plants_animals/living_with_wildlife/0805_emu.pdf Plants & Animals: Emu] * {{Cite news |date=12 November 1932 |title=Attack on Emus |work=The Argus |url=http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article4508317}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:1930s in Western Australia]] [[Category:1932 in Australia]] [[Category:1932 in military history]] [[Category:Agriculture in Western Australia]] [[Category:Australian humour]] [[Category:Dromaius]] [[Category:Emus]] [[Category:History of agriculture in Australia]] [[Category:Non-combat military operations involving Australia]] [[Category:November 1932 in Oceania]] [[Category:Pest control campaigns]] [[Category:December 1932 in Oceania]]
